To evaluate this possibility, we leveraged developments in generative artificial intelligence in two experiments whose primary analyses included 2044 conspiracy believers with complete pretreatment- and post-treatment-belief data after personalized evidence-based dialogues with GPT-4 Turbo.
This separation also preserves CC0 for Dryad data, MIT for code, and existing rights for publication materials.
Study and file scope Participants were assigned to an AI dialogue about a focal conspiracy belief or to an unrelated control dialogue.
The effect remained 2 months later, generalized across a wide range of conspiracy theories, and occurred even among participants with deeply entrenched beliefs.
Although the dialogues focused on a single conspiracy, they nonetheless diminished belief in unrelated conspiracies and shifted conspiracy-related behavioral intentions.

items.title_found: AI succeeds in combatting conspiracy theories | Cornell Chronicle
items.meta_description: Arguing with a conspiracy theorist that the moon landing wasn’t staged is usually a futile effort, but ChatGPT might have better luck, according to new research by Cornell, American University and Massachusetts Institute of Technology psychologists.
passages: To test their theory, Pennycook, Costello and Rand harnessed the power of GPT-4 Turbo, OpenAI’s most advanced large language model, to engage more than 2,000 conspiracy believers in personalized, evidence-based dialogues.

Participants were first asked to identify and describe a conspiracy theory they believed in using their own words, along with the evidence supporting their belief.GPT-4 Turbo then used this information to generate a personalized summary of the participant's belief and initiate a dialogue.
Participants also demonstrated shifts in their behavioral intentions related to conspiracy theories.
“Although much ink has been spilled over the potential for generative AI to supercharge disinformation, our study shows that it can also be part of the solution,” Rand said.

passages: Photo by Christin Hume on Unsplash Using chatbots to reduce conspiracy beliefs – Expert Reaction Expert Reactions | Published: 13 September 202427 October 2026 A new US study* found personalised interactions with a chatbot could reduce belief in conspiracy theories.

Participants who had tailored conversations with a chatbot instructed to “very effectively persuade” them against their conspiracy belief had an average of 20% reduction in these beliefs, which lasted for at least two months.
People reported a lower level of belief in their conspiracy after chatting with the AI bot, even two months later.
